blocks.markdown: **MONDAY  |  From Console to Window: Swing and Safe Startup**

A graphical user interface (GUI) lets a person use windows and controls with a keyboard or mouse. Swing is Java’s built-in toolkit for these controls. AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) supplies older controls, window support, events, and layout tools; Swing builds on AWT [NTU].
The terminal window is the service counter. A label is the sign above it. The event dispatch thread is the clerk who changes signs and handles requests, one short job at a time.
The **event dispatch thread (EDT)** creates and updates the interface and handles its actions. invokeLater queues a job there [NTU] [NUS].
**STEP 1  Show the terminal**
Back up Main.java as Main_week16.txt. Replace Main.java and add TerminalPanel.java. Run.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 5. `System.setProperty("java.awt.headless", "true");` tells Java there is no screen. CodeShare runs your program on a computer with no screen, so no window can open.
- Look at line 6. `System.setProperty("awt.toolkit", "sun.awt.HToolkit");` picks Java's no-screen toolkit, the part of Java that makes controls. With lines 5 and 6, Swing still builds every real control, so we can test them.
- Look at line 7. `SwingUtilities.invokeAndWait` hands the job to the event dispatch thread (EDT), the one thread that may build and change Swing controls, and waits until the job is done.
- Look at line 2 of TerminalPanel.java. `public class TerminalPanel extends JPanel` As you remember from Week 12, extends means TerminalPanel is a JPanel and can do everything a JPanel does. A JPanel is a box that groups controls.
- Look at line 4 of TerminalPanel.java. `add(new JLabel("NXA 123 | Mang Ramon"));` makes a JLabel, a sign that shows text, and adds it to the panel.
- Look at line 5 of TerminalPanel.java. `add(new JLabel("Monumento-Divisoria"));` adds the second sign. The guided example adds a line after this one.
- Look at line 11. `panel.getComponentCount()` counts the controls on the panel: 2.
- Look at line 13. `(JLabel) panel.getComponent(i)` takes control number i. Counting starts at 0, so the first sign is control 0.
- Look at line 18. `if (GraphicsEnvironment.isHeadless())` is true in CodeShare, so line 19 prints the message and line 20 ends main.
- Look at line 24. `new JFrame("Vehicle Terminal")` is the window. It opens only on a computer with a screen, outside CodeShare, with lines 5 and 6 deleted.
- Look at line 25. `JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE` makes the window's close button end the program.

lessons.title: A Click Has a Job: Buttons, Text Fields, and Listeners

objectives.cognitive: Describe how JTextField, JButton, and ActionListener work together when a user clicks.

blocks.markdown: **TUESDAY  |  A Click Has a Job: Buttons, Text Fields, and Listeners**

An event is a report that something happened, such as a click. An ActionListener is an object whose actionPerformed method responds to that report. Register it with addActionListener; otherwise the button has no action [HWS] [MIT].
A button is the bell at a sari-sari store. Ringing it is the event; the listener is the shopkeeper’s agreed response. A bell with no response plan makes noise but serves nobody.

rows: Read a String, even when it contains digits.
Register what happens after a click.
Show a result or helpful feedback.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 3 of TerminalPanel.java. `implements ActionListener` promises an actionPerformed method, so this panel can answer clicks. As you remember from Week 12, an interface is a promise of methods.
- Look at line 4 of TerminalPanel.java. `new JTextField("NXA 123", 8)` a box the user types in. It starts with NXA 123 and is about 8 letters wide.
- Look at line 8 of TerminalPanel.java. `label.setLabelFor(plate);` links the Plate: sign to its box. This helps keyboard and screen-reader users.
- Look at line 10 of TerminalPanel.java. `show.addActionListener(this);` registers the listener: this panel. Without this line a click does nothing.
- Look at line 17 of TerminalPanel.java. `plate.getText().trim()` reads the typed text; trim() removes the spaces at both ends. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 9. `(JTextField) panel.getComponent(1)` The box is control 1, because the Plate: sign is control 0 (line 11 of TerminalPanel.java adds it first).
- Look at line 13. `plate.setText("  TRC 456  ");` types TRC 456 with two spaces on each side.
- Look at line 14. `show.doClick();` clicks Show in code. Swing runs actionPerformed, just as for a mouse click.
- Look at line 15. `result.getText()` shows Plate: TRC 456 with no spaces, because of trim().

blocks.markdown: **WEDNESDAY  |  Reuse the Vehicle Program: Valid Input and Fare Results**
The model holds data and rules: here, the existing Vehicle objects. The interface reads input, calls the model, and displays a result or helpful error [HWS] [NTU].
The service counter does not invent the fare. It asks the existing fare rules, just as our Swing panel asks Vehicle.quoteFare. A misspelled plate should receive a clear reply.

**Validation** checks input before accepting it. Refuse unknown plates and non-numbers. Distance must be finite (neither NaN, “not a number,” nor infinity) and above zero. Fares are classroom practice values, not LTFRB rates.

lessons.title: Keep the Window Responsive: Background Work and Safe Updates

objectives.cognitive: Distinguish interface work from slow work and explain why a listener must return quickly.
objectives.affective: Respect users’ time by keeping the interface available while a slow job runs.
objectives.psychomotor: Create ReadyTask.java and revise Main.java so a background thread reports back through SwingUtilities.invokeLater.

blocks.markdown: **THURSDAY  |  Keep the Window Responsive: Background Work and Safe Updates**

A responsive interface continues to handle actions while work is in progress. A background thread does the slow job. The event dispatch thread (EDT), introduced Monday, handles interface actions and updates. SwingUtilities.invokeLater queues an update on the EDT [NTU] [NUS].
The clerk asks a helper to check a loading bay. The clerk can still answer other customers. The helper returns a report; only the clerk changes the counter sign.

rows: Read fields; disable Check ready; show Checking...; return quickly.
Wait 1 second (simulated slow work), then queue a report.
Later: set readiness text and restore the button.
Never read fields or directly call setText on a visible control.

blocks.markdown: **STEP 7  Wait without freezing the interface**
Add ReadyTask.java and replace Main.java. Keep TerminalPanel.java and FareService.java. Run.

blocks.instruction: Add ReadyTask.java and replace Main.java. Keep TerminalPanel.java and FareService.java. Run.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Before: Not checked
Right after the click: Checking... | button on: false
After the worker: Ready: NXA 123 | button on: true

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 16. `check.setEnabled(false);` turns the button off, so nobody starts a second check while one runs.
- Look at line 18. `new Thread(new ReadyTask(status, check), "Readiness")` As you remember from Week 16, a Runnable job is handed to a Thread, and the thread gets a name.
- Look at line 19. `worker.start();` starts the job on its own thread. actionPerformed then ends at once, so the EDT is free for other clicks.
- Look at line 13 of ReadyTask.java. `Thread.sleep(1000);` the slow job: one second of waiting, on the worker thread, never on the EDT.
- Look at line 14 of ReadyTask.java. `message = "Ready: NXA 123";` the worker's report. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 20 of ReadyTask.java. `SwingUtilities.invokeLater` The worker never changes the sign itself. It queues the change for the EDT.
- Look at line 22 of ReadyTask.java. `status.setText(outcome);` This line runs later, on the EDT.
- Look at line 24. `status.getText()` Right after the click the sign shows Checking... and the button is off. The EDT is still busy with this job, so the worker's queued change cannot run yet. This line prints the same on every computer.
- Look at line 27. `worker.join();` As you remember from Week 16, join() waits for a thread to finish. Here main waits, never the EDT. So the EDT job on line 30 always runs after the worker's queued change.

blocks.markdown: **Main.java**
**ReadyTask.java**
**What happens and why**
The inner listener uses status and check. Main keeps them in static fields, so the EDT jobs and main itself can all reach them.
The worker uses Week 16 Runnable and start(). It sleeps to simulate a slow check, then queues a Runnable on the EDT to update the sign and restore the button.

Interruption is a stop request; ReadyTask restores its flag and reports it. Never make the EDT wait by calling join, await, or sleep in a listener. Main.java line 27 calls join() on the main thread, not the EDT, only so the printed result is always the same.
**Observed console result**

Before: Not checked
Right after the click: Checking... | button on: false
After the worker: Ready: NXA 123 | button on: true

**Why the output never changes:** the click runs on the EDT, so the worker’s queued update must wait until that job ends. Line 24 therefore always shows Checking.... Main then waits for the worker with join() and reads the sign in a new EDT job, after the update. No line depends on how fast the computer is.

**Check yourself.** Change `Thread.sleep(1000);` on line 13 of ReadyTask.java to 2000. Predict the output. (The same three lines: main waits with join(), so the result does not depend on how long the job takes.) Change it back.

**STEP 8  The same job with SwingWorker**
SwingWorker is Swing’s own helper for slow jobs. doInBackground() runs on a worker thread; done() runs afterwards on the EDT, where it may change controls. get() gives the job’s result.
Add ReadyWorker.java and replace Main.java. Keep ReadyTask.java. Run.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 3 of ReadyWorker.java. `extends SwingWorker<String, Void>` SwingWorker is Swing's own helper for slow jobs. String is the type of the job's result.
- Look at line 12 of ReadyWorker.java. `protected String doInBackground()` runs on a worker thread that Swing makes for you. Line 13 is the slow job.
- Look at line 14 of ReadyWorker.java. `return "Ready: NXA 123";` is the job's result. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 16 of ReadyWorker.java. `protected void done()` Swing runs done() on the EDT after doInBackground has finished, so done() may change the sign.
- Look at line 18 of ReadyWorker.java. `status.setText(get());` get() gives the result from line 14. If the job threw an exception, get() throws too, and line 20 shows a polite message.
- Look at line 23 of ReadyWorker.java. `finished.countDown();` As you remember from Week 16, a CountDownLatch counts down to 0 and then lets waiting threads go.
- Look at line 20. `worker.execute();` starts the job. Compare Step 7: no new Thread and no invokeLater. SwingWorker does both for you.
- Look at line 28. `finished.await();` main waits until done() has run. So line 31 always prints after the sign changed, on any computer.
